extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers, research-integrity professionals, and readers interested in retractions and plagiarism issues
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge instances of textual or authorship misconduct in academic publications, including how journals and institutions label/handle such cases (e.g., 'text overlap', 'unacknowledged borrowings', retraction vs correction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: "plagiarism properly so called" vs "unacknowledged borrowings"
rubrics_metrics.description: A report differentiated "plagiarism properly so called" from "unacknowledged borrowings," finding evidence of the latter but not the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions/journals may use finer-grained labels to distinguish types/degree of copying; such distinctions affect whether something is labeled formal plagiarism or a lesser offense and can influence sanctions and public wording in notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Substantial unreferenced overlap"
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices may cite "substantial unreferenced overlap" as the reason for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording signals that large sections of text match prior work and were not properly cited; it's treated as a serious originality breach in retraction statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Citation and attribution errors" (euphemism for plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals sometimes use the phrase "citation and attribution errors" to describe problematic overlap or missing citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog notes this is frequently a euphemism for plagiarism; editors may reach this conclusion after similarity scans (e.g., iThenticate) and when authors cannot adequately explain the overlap, leading to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Text overlap" as a label
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals (e.g., PLOS ONE) may call overlapping fragments "text overlap," even when material was used without credit or quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling something "text overlap" rather than "plagiarism" can change the public characterization and the remedy (e.g., correction vs retraction); however, the underlying factual standard is use of others' text without proper attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Significant overlap" / "borrowing large portions of text"
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices or reports sometimes describe problems as "significant overlap" or that authors "borrowed large portions of text."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These phrasings indicate substantial verbatim or near-verbatim reuse across substantial sections and are treated as grounds for removal or retraction of articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of material "published previously"
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions can cite that the paper used material that was "published previously."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republishing previously published material without appropriate attribution or permission is treated as duplication/plagiarism and can prompt retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of unpublished peer-review material (reviewer stealing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where a peer reviewer 'stole material from an unpublished manuscript' and used it in a later paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using confidential, unpublished material obtained through peer review constitutes serious misconduct separate from textual overlap; it may prompt retraction and institutional investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of co-authors "not involved in the study"
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices sometimes indicate that co-authors were listed who "were not involved in the study."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ghost or guest authorship is an authorship-integrity problem that often accompanies or signals deeper misconduct; it can be cited alongside plagiarism in notices and used as a basis for retraction or correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Improper citation methods" / "breach of warranties ... with respect to originality"
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may phrase the problem as "improper citation methods" and note a "breach of warranties made by the authors with respect to originality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These legalistic/euphemistic formulations indicate failure to meet the publisher's originality assurances; they function as formal grounds for retraction even if the wording avoids the P-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying of titles or first-page material (exact title overlap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices can point to overlap that includes the article's title or first page material as evidence of copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replicating distinctive elements like titles is cited as demonstrative of non-trivial copying and supports retraction decisions and public notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity-detection scores (e.g., high iThenticate scores) as trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors use plagiarism-detection tools (iThenticate) and high similarity scores triggered further investigation and eventual retraction when authors couldn't explain overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity scores are a detection/triage metric; high scores alone require human assessment and author explanation, but unexplained high overlap is treated as strong evidence for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial response calibrated by amount/severity (correction vs retraction vs partial retraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals have varied responses — corrections, partial retractions, retract-and-replacements, or total retraction — depending on the nature and extent of the misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amount and nature of overlap, intent, effect on the scholarly record, and authors' explanations influence whether a correction suffices or a retraction (partial/total) is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of intent (unintentional vs deliberate) but still actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers/institutions may state that errors were believed to be unintentional, yet still remove or stop selling content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent may influence sanction severity and institutional response, but unintentional copying or citation failures can still lead to retraction or other corrective actions.
